question: For a self-attention layer whose score temperature can depend on context length, what asymptotic scaling avoids both uniform-attention rank collapse and an identity-like no-mixing limit, and how does the same transition affect back-propagated gradients?

key_findings.claim: The paper identifies logarithmic score scaling as the critical order in its geometric token model, separating one-step contraction from attention that asymptotically becomes the identity.
key_findings.evidence: Under the regular-simplex assumption with off-diagonal cosine similarity rho and beta_n = gamma log n, Theorem 2.1 places the boundary at gamma = 1/(1-rho). Without a residual branch, subcritical attention sends every pairwise normalized inner product to one, while supercritical attention leaves the original inner product unchanged; the critical point has an intermediate limit.

key_findings.claim: The order-log-n transition persists after relaxing exact simplex symmetry, but the paper proves only separated sufficient regimes rather than a single sharp threshold for general configurations.
key_findings.evidence: Assumption 2 bounds token norms and pairwise similarities between fixed constants. Theorem 2.3 proves strict contraction for gamma below 1/(1-rho_1) and identity-like attention above 1/(1-rho_2); the interval between those bounds is unresolved in the main theorem. A refined three-band score assumption in Appendix C yields an intermediate sparse phase dominated by a subset of high-similarity tokens.

key_findings.claim: The backward-pass analysis exhibits a matching phase change: subcritical attention has vanishing average squared Jacobian singular value, whereas supercritical attention retains a nonzero normalization-map contribution.
key_findings.evidence: With the residual contribution removed by setting alpha to zero, Theorem 2.4 gives normalized Jacobian Frobenius norm tending to zero below the simplex threshold, 1/(4q)(1-1/d) at the threshold, and 1/q(1-1/d) above it. Theorem 2.5 gives corresponding upper and lower bounds for almost-simplex inputs, and identifies the leading supercritical block Jacobian with the derivative of token normalization.

key_findings.claim: Synthetic single-layer simulations agree qualitatively with the predicted angle and gradient transitions and show that finite low dimension smooths the sharp simplex boundary.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment samples correlated Gaussian tokens, varies rho, gamma, and d, and measures average input-to-output angle ratio plus a Hutchinson estimate of the normalized Jacobian norm. At d=512 both plots transition near gamma = 1/(1-rho); at d=2 and d=32 the random spread in pairwise similarities creates a broader partial-interaction region.

anchors.section: 3 Numerical Experiments, sampling model and angle metric

key_findings.claim: The logarithmic law is not universal across score ensembles: it follows from an order-one top-score gap, while Gaussian random-energy scores yield a square-root-log critical scale.
key_findings.evidence: The main geometric assumptions keep the decisive similarity gaps at order one, so balancing exp(beta times gap) against n alternatives gives beta of order log n. Appendix D shows that extreme Gaussian score gaps shrink as 1/sqrt(log n), giving beta of order sqrt(log n), consistent with the random-energy analysis the paper contrasts against.

key_findings.claim: The results do not yet validate logarithmic scaling in a trained long-context language model or establish an optimal constant for practical attention heads.
key_findings.evidence: Every theorem studies one simplified pre-normalized attention map with K=Q=V=I and fixed positive pairwise similarities; the numerical section uses the same one-layer correlated-Gaussian construction and omits residual connections and MLPs. There are no language-model loss, retrieval, context extrapolation, or multi-head ablations, so the claimed justification for YaRN, Qwen, SSMax, and SWAN-GPT is order-of-growth support under a model, not direct empirical validation of those systems.

method.core_idea: Analyze softmax temperature as an asymptotic competition between a token's self-score and the multiplicity of off-diagonal scores, then track how the winning scale changes normalized token angles and the layer Jacobian.
method.mechanism: The paper fixes K, Q, and V to identity, normalizes tokens before attention, and studies beta_n-scaled cosine scores. Exact simplex symmetry permits closed-form softmax and angle limits; bounded almost-simplex geometry gives uniform asymptotic bounds; matrix-calculus estimates characterize the normalized Jacobian; correlated-Gaussian simulations test the predicted forward and backward transitions.
assumptions: Token norms and non-self cosine similarities remain within fixed positive bounds as context length grows.
The query, key, and value matrices are identities and the analysis represents a single attention head.
Score-gap geometry, rather than only score variance, controls the relevant temperature scale.
The residual branch can be separated from the attention Jacobian when diagnosing gradient flow.
One-layer correlated-Gaussian token simulations are an informative check of the asymptotic theory.

techniques.role: Sets beta_n = gamma log n and treats gamma as the phase-control parameter.
Makes all off-diagonal scores equal so forward limits can be calculated exactly.
Extends the scaling order to non-equiangular, lower-dimensional token sets.
Uses the mean squared singular value to diagnose gradient collapse or survival.
Numerically estimates the large layer Jacobian norm in synthetic experiments.

evaluations.setting: Single attention layer on correlated Gaussian tokens x_i = sqrt(rho) z_0 + sqrt(1-rho) z_i across d=2, 32, and 512
evaluations.metric: Average ratio of output angular distance to input angular distance
evaluations.result: Contraction at low gamma, near-identity behavior at high gamma, and an increasingly sharp boundary near 1/(1-rho) as dimension increases
evaluations.baseline: Theorem 2.1 simplex asymptotic boundary and Theorem 2.3 bounded transition interval

evaluations.setting: The same synthetic configurations with automatic Jacobian-vector computations
evaluations.metric: Normalized squared Frobenius norm of the input-output Jacobian estimated by Hutchinson's method
evaluations.result: Near zero below the transition and near 1-1/d above it, with a smoothed intermediate region at small d

limitations: The analyzed layer fixes K=Q=V=I, excludes MLPs and multi-head interactions, and only indirectly represents a trained transformer.
Positive, context-length-independent similarity bounds exclude many realistic signed or near-orthogonal score geometries.
The main almost-simplex theorem leaves a gap between sufficient subcritical and supercritical constants.
The experiments validate the stylized model, not language-model training, retrieval, perplexity, or length extrapolation.
Residual connections are discussed in the forward map but removed for the headline Jacobian phase results.
failure_modes: Below the critical scale, attention becomes diffuse and contracts token representations toward rank collapse.
Above the critical scale, self-attention approaches the identity and ceases meaningful cross-token mixing.
In the subcritical regime the attention-path Jacobian can vanish, leaving learning dependent on residual paths.
A temperature rule transferred to a different score-gap distribution can use the wrong asymptotic scale.
Finite-dimensional heterogeneous scores can blur the predicted sharp threshold into a broad intermediate phase.
reusable_insights: Temperature scaling should be derived from the extreme-gap statistics of actual head scores, not context length alone.
A useful attention diagnostic jointly measures token angular contraction, attention entropy, off-diagonal mass, and Jacobian scale.
The desirable operating region is a sparse but nondegenerate interaction phase, rather than merely maximizing attention concentration.
Phase-boundary claims should be stress-tested across score ensembles because order-one and Gaussian extreme gaps imply different laws.
open_questions: What are the empirical top-score-gap scalings of trained attention heads across layers, tasks, and context lengths?
Can a head-wise adaptive temperature maintain both cross-token information flow and stable gradients without knowing the eventual context length?
Does the intermediate sparse phase improve downstream loss or retrieval compared with SSMax, YaRN, and fixed-temperature baselines?
How do learned K/Q projections, causal masks, rotary embeddings, residual scaling, and MLP blocks move the transition?
Can the almost-simplex gap between subcritical and supercritical constants be closed under realistic score-distribution assumptions?

competitive_landscape.title: Two failure modes of deep transformers and how to avoid them: a unified theory of signal propagation at initialisation
competitive_landscape.difference: Uses a random-energy treatment of full transformer blocks and analyzes both rank and entropy collapse at initialization; its Gaussian extreme-score model produces a different critical scaling and its latest version includes three architecture case studies.

competitive_landscape.title: Scalable-Softmax Is Superior for Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Introduces log-length-scaled softmax and evaluates language-model pretraining, long-context retrieval, and post-hoc replacement, while the present paper supplies geometric asymptotic theory but no trained-language-model evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Geometric Dynamics of Signal Propagation Predict Trainability of Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Tracks depth-wise order-chaos geometry and Lyapunov exponents in randomly initialized attention-plus-MLP transformers, whereas the present work varies context length and softmax temperature for a simplified single attention map.

competitive_landscape.title: Quantitative Clustering in Mean-Field Transformer Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Proves long-time exponential synchronization rates for continuous mean-field transformer dynamics; the present work instead studies a context-length-dependent one-layer transition and the identity-like over-scaling failure.

competitive_landscape.title: YaRN: Efficient Context Window Extension of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Combines rotary-position interpolation and attention-temperature scaling to extend pretrained LLM contexts; it offers system evidence but does not isolate the geometric phase law proved in the present stylized model.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A rigorous critical beta_n proportional to log n explains why practical long-context methods scale attention scores polylogarithmically and reveals matching forward and backward phase transitions.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact simplex calculation, almost-simplex bounds, Jacobian theorems, and synthetic sweeps all support an order-log-n transition when decisive score gaps remain order one.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty is the explicit geometric score-gap explanation and paired Jacobian result. It complements rather than supersedes random-energy and system work: the scale is model-dependent, and practical optimality remains untested.
